ci1.title: CI Principiante
ci1.promise: Your first Italian, taught in Rome — the city where the language began. In twenty live lessons you go from the sound of the language to your first real conversations.
outcomes: Introduce yourself, family and work in Italian
Order food, coffee and drinks with confidence
Understand slow, clear spoken Italian in daily situations
Handle numbers, dates, times and money
Write short messages and postcards in Italian
Read menus, signs and simple posts
syllabus: The Italian sound system, greetings, subject pronouns, the verb essere. Set at Fiumicino, first steps in Rome.
Introducing yourself, nationalities, avere, definite articles. A dialogue at a Roman café.
Family vocabulary, possessive adjectives, plural nouns. Photos from a real Roman family.
Ordering coffee, present tense of regular verbs (-are), c'è / ci sono. The espresso ritual.
Prepositions of place, andare and venire, asking for directions. The seven hills of Rome.
Telling time, days of the week, months, the verb fare. A day in the life of a Roman.
Food vocabulary, partitives, quanto costa, ordering in a trattoria. Cucina romana.
Piacere, opinions, comparatives, likes and dislikes. Italian film and music.
Weather, seasons, dovere / potere / volere. Weekends in the Roman countryside.
Rooms of the house, furniture, dare and stare. Roman apartment life.
Clothes, colours, adjectives that agree, sapere vs conoscere. Via del Corso, the shopping street.
Food shopping, markets, imperative for polite requests. Campo de' Fiori.
Work vocabulary, jobs, telefonare, scrivere. A day in a Roman office.
Trains, tickets, hotels, the near future with andare a + infinitive. Termini Station.
Review, mini test, oral presentation. Half-way milestone.
Introduction to the past tense with avere. Yesterday in Rome.
The past with essere, agreement of the past participle. Stories from a Sunday.
Describing places, reflexive verbs, daily routine. Trastevere on a Saturday.
Weekend plans, imperfetto introduced, contrastive with passato. A country outing.
Full oral CEFR A1.1 assessment, farewell dialogue, next steps. Ready for CI Elementare.

ci2.title: CI Elementare
ci2.promise: Everyday Italian from Florence, the city where the language was standardised. Twenty live lessons that take you from short replies to full daily narrative.
outcomes: Narrate a past event or weekend in detail
Describe people, places and things with precision
Make and change plans on the phone
Handle emails and short letters in Italian
Understand a Tuscan waiter, shopkeeper or landlord
Read simple newspaper headlines and short articles
syllabus: Why Italian is Tuscan. Dante, Boccaccio, Petrarch. Review of A1.1.
Passato prossimo consolidation, time markers (ieri, la settimana scorsa).
Imperfetto for description and habit, comparison with passato prossimo.
Describing people physically and in character. Adjective agreement in depth.
Rooms, prepositions of place, ci per luogo. A Florentine apartment tour.
Regional food vocabulary, ne partitivo, cooking verbs. Ribollita, bistecca, cantucci.
Full dining dialogue, complaining politely, tipping, il conto per favore.
Phone conventions, formal register, leaving a message.
Making appointments — doctor, hairdresser, notary. The Italian bureaucratic register.
Body vocabulary, at the pharmacy, common ailments, mi fa male + body part.
Reflexive verbs, morning routine, adverbs of frequency.
Hobbies, sport, Serie A football, Sunday papers.
Fellini and Sorrentino, film vocabulary, expressing opinion.
Midpoint review, oral test, cultural quiz on Florence.
Simple future tense, plans, promises, predictions.
Introduction to hypothetical: se + present / future, se + imperfetto / condizionale (light touch).
Condizionale for polite requests and wishes: vorrei, mi piacerebbe, potrei.
Email conventions, formal vs informal register, greetings and sign-offs.
CEFR A1.2 full assessment, cultural presentation, path to CI Intermedio.

ci3.title: CI Intermedio
ci3.promise: Confident daily Italian from Bologna — la Dotta, la Grassa, la Rossa. Twenty live lessons on tenses, opinion, argument and the language of the Italian table.
outcomes: Move between passato prossimo, imperfetto and trapassato with ease
Express opinion, doubt and preference clearly
Talk about food, cooking, cuisine and regional identity
Understand fast native speech in most everyday situations
Read blogs, restaurant reviews and short essays
Take part in a small group conversation for the full 85 minutes
syllabus: Italy's oldest university, the arcades, the food. Review of A1.2.
Recognising passato remoto in fairy tales and news. Passive knowledge only.
Talking about what happened before what happened. Storytelling structure.
The Italian storytelling engine. Real narratives from a Bolognese childhood.
Ragù, tortellini, mortadella, Parmigiano. Cooking verbs and cultural vocabulary.
Dinner-party Italian. Interrupting politely, agreeing, disagreeing, refilling wine.
Expressing opinion: penso che, credo che, secondo me. Congiuntivo introduced softly.
Comparing places: più / meno / così… come. Bologna vs Milano vs Roma.
Reserving tickets, film genres, describing a plot, recommending.
Lucio Dalla, Battisti, De Andrè, contemporary indie. Listening lab.
Hypothetical in the present: se + congiuntivo imperfetto + condizionale.
Describing Italian cities, geography, north / centre / south differences.
Vocabulary of work, CV, colloquio di lavoro, contratti.
Healthcare vocabulary, at the doctor, at the hospital, the Italian public system.
Bank vocabulary, opening an account, paying bills, ordering online.
Renting an apartment, understanding a contract, negotiating with a landlord.
Italian holidays: Natale, Pasqua, Ferragosto, Palio di Siena, Carnevale di Venezia.
Introduction to Italian dialects — bolognese, romanesco, napoletano, siciliano — as cultural heritage.
Full CEFR A2.1 assessment, oral presentation, path to CI Avanzato.

ci4.title: CI Avanzato
ci4.promise: Real Italian for real life, between the warmth of Naples and the sharpness of Milan. Twenty live lessons that consolidate CEFR A2 and open the door to B1.
outcomes: Use congiuntivo in context, not just in tests
Follow a fast Italian film without subtitles most of the time
Argue, persuade and negotiate in a small-group setting
Write structured emails, reviews and short articles
Understand regional accents from north to south
Sit and pass an internationally recognised A2 exam
syllabus: The northern-southern axis of Italian identity. Review of A2.1.
Full introduction to the subjunctive: after verbs of opinion, doubt, feeling.
Backshift, hypothetical use, se + imperfetto + condizionale.
Reported speech: he said that…, she asked whether…
Reading Corriere della Sera and la Repubblica. Newspaper Italian.
Full film analysis: La Grande Bellezza, La Vita è Bella, Il Postino.
Understanding a Verdi libretto. Aria listening lab.
Meeting vocabulary, presenting, negotiating, closing a deal.
Institutions, parties, elections — the vocabulary of civic life.
Full midpoint oral, written and listening assessment.
Debating in Italian. Structured arguments, giving and refuting points.
The language of sales, marketing and advertising. Rhetorical devices.
Napoletano expressions that entered standard Italian. Neapolitan cinema.
Milanese business register, aperitivo culture, fashion vocabulary.
Ferrante, Calvino, Baricco — reading passages and discussion.
Twenty regions, twenty cuisines — a culinary tour of Italy.
Italian education from elementari to università, plus the language of academia.
Practical language for moving to Italy: codice fiscale, permesso di soggiorno, sanità.
The language of jure sanguinis, applications, consular Italian.
Full CEFR A2.2 assessment, cultural graduation, path to B1.

ps1.title: Al Caffè
ps1.promise: Twenty live conversation sessions set at Italian cafés. No grammar drills, no textbooks — only spoken Italian, from the first minute.
outcomes: Order coffee, food and drinks with cultural confidence
Small-talk with a barista, a neighbour or a taxi driver
Understand the fast, warm rhythm of café Italian
Handle greetings, farewells and social pleasantries
React naturally with typical Italian interjections
Speak Italian without stopping to translate in your head
syllabus: The espresso ritual — every word that happens at a Roman bar.
Standing at the bar vs sitting at the table. Prices, timing, tipping.
Meeting the same barista every morning. The Italian art of daily kindness.
Small talk with the person next to you at the bar.
Football at the bar. Every man and woman in Italy has an opinion.
Politics at the bar — how to nod, agree, and not commit.
When you are addressed in English — how to reply, gently, in Italian.
Ordering breakfast. Sweet vs savoury, cream vs jam, the difference between un cornetto and un croissant.
Midpoint conversation lab — a full 15-minute unstructured chat with the teacher.
Ordering a quick lunch — panino, tramezzino, insalatona.
The Milanese ritual — spritz, negroni, and the vocabulary of small plates.
Paying the bill. Coperto, servizio, mancia. Splitting the bill Italian-style.
Take-away Italian — a very recent phenomenon that has its own new vocabulary.
Sunday breakfast at a bar — bombolone, sfogliatella, maritozzo.
Office caffè culture — the coffee run, the machine, the coffee gossip.
Grandmother's moka pot. The most sacred coffee of all.
Hotel breakfast Italian — buffet vs à la carte, the polite requests.
Summer at the beach bar. Granita, gelato, spremuta d'arancia.
Final oral conversation, cultural graduation, path to A Tavola.

ps2.title: A Tavola
ps2.promise: Twenty live conversation sessions set at the Italian table. Order like a Roman, argue like a Neapolitan about pasta shape, and understand a Tuscan grandmother.
outcomes: Read any Italian menu without pointing
Ask for a table, a wine, a dish, and a change — politely
Understand a waiter's rapid recitation of the specials
Argue politely about a dish or a bill
Talk about food history, region and cuisine
Cook and talk in Italian at the same time
syllabus: Reading a full Italian menu: antipasto, primo, secondo, contorno, dolce.
Booking a table by phone. Time, number of people, dietary needs.
Ordering wine. Regional grape varieties, house wine vs bottle, the sommelier.
Bruschetta, salumi, formaggi — Italy's opening course in every region.
Pasta shapes and their sauces. The rules that Italians never break.
Meat, fish, vegetarian, contorno pairing. Regional traditions.
Tiramisù, panna cotta, cannolo — and the sacred espresso after.
Talking to the owner. The Italian art of building a relationship with the trattoria.
Buying at the market — asking the fishmonger, the greengrocer, the butcher.
Midpoint full conversational assessment set in a virtual trattoria.
Home cooking Italian — la nonna, la mamma, la ricetta di famiglia.
Cooking together in real time — verbs of preparation, quantities, timings.
Ordering a pizza. Neapolitan vs Roman vs alla pala. The rules of margherita.
Ordering gelato — sizes, flavours, cono vs coppa, panna sì o no.
Italian food festivals — the sagra del tartufo, della porchetta, dell'oliva.
High-end restaurant Italian. Michelin-star register, degustazione.
Neighbourhood trattoria Italian — the friendly regular.
Cappuccino after 11 am? Never. Parmigiano on seafood? Never. The rules.
Paying the bill. Splitting Italian-style, tipping, the ricevuta fiscale.
Final oral, cultural graduation, path to In Viaggio.

ps3.title: In Viaggio
ps3.promise: Twenty live conversation sessions for people who actually travel Italy — trains, hotels, museums, mountain refuges, sailing the Amalfi coast.
outcomes: Handle any Italian train, plane or bus without English
Check in and out of any Italian hotel or B&B
Ask for and understand directions in old-town labyrinths
Talk to museum staff, art historians and gallerists
Navigate an Italian pharmacy and doctor's office
Understand regional accents from Bolzano to Palermo
syllabus: Buying a ticket at Termini, Trenitalia vs Italo, first vs second class.
Italian train vocabulary. Coincidence, ritardo, il capotreno.
Check-in, security, boarding, delays — Italian airport register.
Taxi Italian — meter, tipping, negotiating an out-of-town ride.
Hotel check-in and check-out. Requesting a room change, room service, breakfast.
Bed & breakfast Italian — meeting the host, house rules, breakfast conversations.
Renting a private apartment — codes, keys, house manuals, neighbour relations.
Museum Italian — audio guide, guided tour, understanding a wall label.
Exhibition Italian — talking to a curator, buying the catalogue, opinion.
Midpoint full oral assessment set on a virtual Italian trip.
Pharmacy Italian — describing symptoms, over-the-counter medicine, prescriptions.
At the doctor — the appointment, the visit, the referral.
Emergency room Italian — the codes, the triage, the paperwork.
Bank Italian — changing money, opening an account, ATM problems.
Post office Italian — sending a package, paying a bill, buying stamps.
Autogrill Italian — the fast lunch on the motorway, ordering at the counter.
Mountain Italian — rifugio, sentiero, guida alpina, mal di montagna.
Beach Italian — lettino, ombrellone, bagnino, cabina.
Urban Italian — public transport, ZTL, parking, the metro in Rome, Milan, Naples.
Final oral, cultural graduation, path to Chiacchierando.

ps4.title: Chiacchierando
ps4.promise: Twenty live conversation sessions on the four things Italians actually do all day: opinion, humour, disagreement and storytelling. This is where confidence becomes fluency.
outcomes: Hold a full 30-minute Italian conversation on any everyday topic
Express opinion, doubt, sarcasm and humour
Disagree politely and change someone's mind
Tell a story with structure, pacing and punchline
Understand rapid native banter and jokes
Sit and pass an internationally recognised B1 oral exam
syllabus: What chiacchierare really means. The philosophy of unhurried talk.
Storytelling structure — introduction, complication, punchline. Italian narrative style.
Italian humour — the setup, the beat, the payoff. Regional humour.
Football arguments. Fifteen minutes on Juve vs Milan and no one leaves offended.
Political conversation — how to hold a strong opinion without breaking a friendship.
Family talk — the mother-in-law joke, the cousin gossip, the Sunday lunch.
Work talk — complaining, bragging, gossiping about the boss.
Money talk — Italy's ambiguity around money. What is said and what is meant.
Love talk — flirting, breaking up, staying friends. The vocabulary of the heart.
Full midpoint conversation lab — 30-minute unstructured chat with the teacher.
Gossip Italian — the register, the euphemisms, the raised eyebrow.
The Italian art of complaining — bureaucratic, personal, existential.
Giving advice in Italian — what to say, what to never say.
Real disagreement — how to argue and still finish the meal together.
Making up in Italian — the words, the gestures, the coffee that follows.
Stand-up Italian — analyzing a comedian's routine and trying one yourself.
Watching a real Italian talk show together. Register, interrupting, humour.
Listening to a real Italian podcast, then discussing it in Italian for 40 minutes.
Being interviewed and interviewing — a full role-play in Italian.
Final CEFR B1 oral assessment, graduation ceremony, path to advanced study.

cap-food.title: La Cucina — The Language of the Italian Table
cap-food.promise: Six live cultural sessions on the vocabulary and history of the Italian table — pasta, pane, vino, caffè, and the sacred rituals of the family meal.
outcomes: Read any Italian recipe with confidence
Understand a regional Italian menu at a glance
Talk knowledgeably about pasta shape, sauce and region
Discuss the history of Italian coffee, wine and olive oil
Understand the ritual grammar of the Italian Sunday lunch
Order, cook and discuss food in Italian at a cultured level
syllabus: How Italy's twenty regions produced twenty cuisines. The north-south axis of butter vs olive oil, rice vs pasta, wine vs beer.
La pasta — mille forme, mille storie
Four hundred pasta shapes. Why bucatini all'amatriciana can only be bucatini. The unwritten pasta rules.
The vocabulary of bread — pane sciapo, pagnotta, michetta, focaccia. The village bakery as institution.
Twenty regions, twenty wine cultures. Reading a label, understanding DOC and DOCG, the ritual of the tasting.
The Italian relationship with coffee, from Trieste to Naples. The bar, the moka, the caffettiera.
The most sacred meal in Italian life. Six courses, three hours, one grandmother. Cultural graduation.

cap-art.title: L'Arte — Renaissance in the Words That Made It
cap-art.promise: Six live cultural sessions on the Italian language of art history — from Giotto to Caravaggio — with the vocabulary that lets you read a museum wall label in the Uffizi.
outcomes: Read a full Italian museum wall label without translation
Understand a Uffizi or Vatican Museums audio guide
Talk about painting, sculpture and architecture in Italian
Grasp the terminology of the Italian Renaissance
Discuss Caravaggio, Michelangelo, Raphael and Bernini in their own language
Take an Italian guided tour with confidence
syllabus: The Italian vocabulary of painting — tela, tavola, affresco, tempera, olio, sfumato, chiaroscuro.
Giotto and the birth of Western perspective. The vocabulary of pre-Renaissance devotion.
Brunelleschi, Donatello, Botticelli. Reading Vasari on the Uffizi masters.
Michelangelo, Raphael, Bramante. The Sistine Chapel and Saint Peter's in their own vocabulary.
The Caravaggio revolution — luce, ombra, realismo. Reading a Bellori page.
Bernini's Rome — Piazza Navona, Piazza San Pietro, the language of Baroque sculpture. Cultural graduation.

cap-opera.title: L'Opera — Opera as a Second Language
cap-opera.promise: Six live cultural sessions on Verdi, Puccini and Rossini. Read a libretto, follow an aria, and understand why Italians still cry at La Scala.
outcomes: Read a Verdi or Puccini libretto in Italian
Follow an aria and grasp its meaning in real time
Understand the vocabulary of opera — voci, ruoli, registri, ripiene
Talk about opera history from the Camerata to Verismo
Attend a live opera and understand the plot without subtitles
Discuss a performance in Italian with a fellow enthusiast
syllabus: Florence, 1600 — the Camerata de' Bardi and the invention of opera. Vocabulary of stagecraft.
Reading and singing along to Largo al factotum. Comic opera vocabulary.
Reading Libiamo ne' lieti calici. Verdi as national poet.
The political operas. Va, pensiero as second national anthem.
Reading Che gelida manina. The verismo revolution and the vocabulary of Parisian bohemia.
Reading Nessun dorma. The final Puccini opera and its cultural afterlife. Cultural graduation.
